newsitem.title: USA: World pact could weaken US food safety, group says.
newsitem.headline: World pact could weaken US food safety, group says.

text.p: U.S. nutrition groups expressed concern on Tuesday that international food safety standards proposed by Australia and other countries could weaken U.S. food safety laws.

At a news conference, representatives from the Center for Science in the Public Interest and the Community Nutrition Institute urged U.S. negotiators to block several proposals slated for discussion next week in Geneva.
One proposal being advanced by Australia would establish self-inspection of meat by packing facilities as equivalent to government inspection, the groups said.

If accepted next week by the Codex Alimentarius, an international organization charged with setting food safety standards, the U.S. would be forced to accept company-inspected meat from Australia, even though U.S. law requires government inspection, the group said.
USDA Spokesman Jim Petterson said he was unable to comment on the group's charges because key department officials were already on their way to Geneva for the discussions.

However, another USDA aide, who asked not to be identified, said the U.S is allowed under international trade rules to have "more stringent standards" than contained in the Codex as long as it provides "a scientific basis" for those standards.
The nutrition groups also expressed concern about other proposals that they said they United States could be forced to accept:
-- unpasteurized cheese and other dairy products, even though the Food and Drug Administration banned such products in 1987 after they caused a number of deaths and illnesses
--bottled mineral water with lower levels of minerals than those required by the Food and Drug Administration
--food additives not approved by the FDA for use in the United States
--fruit juices, milk and other foods containing higher lead contents than U.S. standards allow
